claims.text: Local lattice distortions induced by atomic-size mismatch primarily govern hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys.
Atomic-size-mismatch-induced lattice distortions impede dislocation motion.
Composition can be varied to produce HEAs with different atomic size mismatches while retaining the same phase structure and grain size.
Identical mechanical processing will ensure similar grain sizes and texture across the samples.
Local lattice distortions act as obstacles to dislocation movement.
Larger atomic size mismatches increase lattice distortions.
Increased lattice distortion enhances dislocation pinning.
Enhanced dislocation pinning raises the stress required for dislocation movement.
A higher stress required for dislocation movement increases hardness and yield strength through solid-solution strengthening.
HEAs with greater atomic size mismatch will have significantly higher hardness than baseline HEAs with minimal atomic size mismatch.
HEAs with greater atomic size mismatch will have significantly higher yield strength than baseline HEAs with minimal atomic size mismatch.
The proposed relationship is limited to single-phase, equiatomic or near-equiatomic HEAs without phase separation, significant precipitation, or dominant grain-boundary effects.
The proposed relationship may not apply at extreme temperatures because thermal activation alters dislocation dynamics.
Grain-boundary strengthening, short-range ordering, and secondary-phase formation can also contribute to HEA hardness and strength.
Diffraction and microscopy can be used to quantify lattice distortion and assess microstructural uniformity in the proposed samples.
